## Atomic scale etching of diamond: insights from molecular dynamics simulations

Jack S Draney1, Joseph R Vella2, Athanassios Z Panagiotopoulos1 and David B Graves1,∗

1 Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540, United States of America 2 Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ 08540, United States of America

E-mail: dgraves@princeton.edu

Received 19 March 2024, revised 31 July 2024 Accepted for publication 10 September 2024 Published 16 October 2024

Abstract Diamond is a promising material for multiple applications in quantum information processing and sensing as well as applications in microelectronics. However, diamond devices can be limited by surface defects that compromise charge stability and spin coherence, among others. Improved strategies in plasma etching of diamond could play an important role in minimizing or eliminating these defects. In this work, we explore plasma-assisted atomic scale etching of diamond using argon ions (Ar+), hydrogen ions (H+) and hydrogen atoms (H). We employ classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and test several interatomic potentials based on the Reactive Empirical Bond Order (REBO) form with comparisons to a variety of published experimental results. We performed MD simulations of low-energy hydrogen (⩽50 eV) and argon (⩽200 eV) ion bombardment of diamond surfaces. Ar+ bombardment can be used to locally smooth initially rough diamond surfaces via the formation of an amorphous C layer, the thickness of which increases with argon ion energy. Subsequent exposure with hydrogen ions (or fast neutrals) will selectively etch this amorphous C layer, leaving the underlying diamond layer mostly intact if the H energy is maintained below about 10 eV. The simulations suggest that combining Ar+ smoothing with selective, near threshold energy H removal of amorphous C can be an effective strategy for diamond surface engineering, leading to more reliable and sensitive diamond color center devices.

make functional devices. Controlling diamond surface chemistry is difficult because of its relative chemical inertness and due to challenges in preparing flat diamond surfaces with uniform properties. Diamond surfaces are typically mechanically polished after growth to obtain smooth surfaces, but the resulting surface is highly strained to depths of several microns [3]. Subsequent conventional plasma etching (sometimes referred to as reactive ion etching or RIE) will remove this strained layer, but plasma etching can be difficult to control and can result in major variability in surface morphology and surface termination. This is an especially serious problem in the case of diamond surfaces to be used for quantum sensing because of the extreme sensitivity of the resulting devices to even a few nearby atomic scale defects [1–4]. The current best practices in color center device processing after RIE involve the use of a combination of vacuum annealing over many hours, followed by hot acid cleaning [3]. More annealing and acid cleaning steps may be used following subsequent ion implantation for dopant incorporation. However, even utilizing the current best practices in surface engineering, coherence times of shallow NV centers remain far from typical bulk values. There is a clear need to better understand plasma-diamond surface interactions in order to exploit the many potential strengths of plasma processing for this promising class of materials. The present article reports results from classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of argon ion (Ar+), hydrogen atoms (H) and hydrogen ions (H+) impacting diamond carbon (C) surfaces. The first set of studies reported here aim to assess the ability of the MD simulation protocol and the associated interatomic potentials to match the available experimental data. We examine published measurements of Ar+ impacting a diamond surface, creating an amorphous layer and physically sputtering C. Additional comparisons are made between measurements and MD simulations for etching hard hydrocarbon films with a combination of Ar+ and atomic H. Finally, we compare the available experimental data and MD simulation results for energetic H+ ions impacting graphitic carbon. As with virtually all plasma–surface interactions, impacts by Ar+ or H+ ions can significantly alter the near-surface properties in a variety of ways. In our study, we highlight the effects of Ar+ bombardment on diamond, creating an amorphous C region near the surface and how this can be utilized for local surface smoothing. H+ impacts from hyperthermal to 10 eV are shown to etch this amorphous carbon more rapidly than the underlying diamond, suggesting a possible processing protocol that can result in near-perfect diamond surfaces. We illustrate one version of this idea by showing how a sequential Ar+ amorphization followed by H+ hydrogenation and selective etching scheme can result in removal of most of the plasmagenerated near-surface damaged layer. This sequence is shown to leave only about one monolayer of damaged, hydrogenated carbon on the diamond surface. The present results illustrate how careful control of plasma processes and plasma–surface interactions will be needed to more fully exploit plasma for critical applications such as diamond color center device processing. The range of possible

conditions and plasma chemistries that can be utilized is large and the field is in need of systematic studies combining experiment and computation. Atomistic simulations of plasma–surface interactions such as those presented here will be most useful when combined with well-defined and controlled plasma, material and surface science experiments.

## 2. Methods

2.1. Setup

Simulations are performed with the LAMMPS [5] simulation package (version 29 December 2022) using the inbuilt ‘rebo’ style for the second-generation REBO potential [6] (REBO2) and the REBO2-S potential from Atomistica library v1.1.0 for the screened REBO potential developed by Pastweka et al [7] (REBO2-S). Many of the simulations were also repeated with the first generation REBO potential [8, 9] (REBO1) and AIREBO [10] in order to provide comparisons between a variety of REBO style potentials. Etch yields for these auxiliary potentials are reported in SI figure S1. Interactions with argon were modeled with the ZBL potential [11]. Ions are simulated as uncharged atoms, as it is assumed the ions are Auger neutralized before impact [12]. Treatment of H+ ions and H atoms differs only in terms of their initial velocities: incident H+ ions are given large velocities normal to the surface, while H atoms are introduced with velocities sampled from the Maxwell– Boltzmann distribution at the temperature of interest. Simulations performed on diamond substrates begin with a bare 2×1 reconstructed (001) surface. The boundary conditions are periodic in the x and y directions and ‘shrinkwrapped’ in the z direction, meaning the boundaries are fixed at some minimum distance but allowed to increase temporarily if atoms move beyond this distance, ensuring no atoms are lost. Simulation cells have varying surface areas, with the primary cell sizes being 6 unit cells by 6 unit cells in the x and y directions (hereafter referred to as the 6 × 6 cell) and 10 unit cells by 10 unit cells in the x and y directions (10 × 10). These correspond to areas of approximately 4.6 × 10−14 cm2 for the (6 × 6) cell and 1.27 × 10−13 cm2 for the (10 × 10) case. The total number of atoms in each simulation varies, but typically 6 × 6 cells contain 1000–3000 atoms, while 10 ×10 cells contain around 5000 atoms. Amorphous substrates are prepared by bombarding diamond surfaces with 200 eV Ar+ ions until steady state is reached. The lattice constant for each potential is set to the value that minimizes the potential energy of a diamond lattice at 0 K. Diamond’s low thermal expansion coefficient means the equilibrium lattice constant is negligibly higher around 300 K, where these simulations were performed, so this 0 K lattice constant is acceptable. The bottom two layers of the cell are fixed in place to prevent the cell from moving and to simulate a continuous diamond layer below.

high enough that it is outside the interaction range of the potential, with a velocity normal to the surface corresponding to the ion energy of interest. The angular distribution of ions is not considered. The simulation is then integrated in the microcanonical ensemble (the energy, cell volume, and number of particles are conserved) using an adaptive timestep for 0.5 ps in the case of REBO2 and 1 ps in the case of REBO2- S. Increasing this time to 1 ps for REBO2 had no significant effect. An adaptive timestep is necessary, because the low mass and high velocity of incoming hydrogen ions leads to poor conservation of energy unless the timstep is on the order of 10−6 ps during the initial impact. An adaptive timestep allows the simulation to maintain this small timestep for the initial impact and then relax to a longer timestep once the ion has lost some of its kinetic energy. The adaptive timestep is set such that the fastest atom only moves 0.01 Å every step, but is restricted to a maximum value of 0.25 fs. Following the ion impact, any clusters which satisfy the following three conditions are removed and recorded: (i) they have detached from the surface by moving all their atoms outside the interaction range of the potential, (ii) they have a center of mass above the highest surface atom and (iii) they have a center of mass with a positive z velocity (directed away from the surface). If the incident ion is argon it is also removed at this point under the assumption that it would desorb during the inter-impact time in a real system. After this, a stratified Berendsen thermostat [13] as described by Vella and Graves [14] is applied for 0.5 ps with a constant timestep of 0.25 fs. The use of the Berendsen thermostat is justified in this case, as its purpose is to remove the excess energy deposited by the ion before the next ion impact, approximating the effect of the inter-impact cooling time. Because the reactions of interest are primarily ion-driven rather than thermally-driven, a perfect Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of energies is not necessary, and a Berendsen thermostat is sufficient. In simulations of simultaneous Ar+/H bombardment, the surface temperature is kept at 340 K to match the related experiments by Hopf et al [15]. In all other simulations, the surface temperature is kept at 300 K. After the application of the thermostat, detached clusters are again removed. At this point, if the number of carbon atoms is less than the initial number of carbon atoms in the simulation, layers of diamond are added to the bottom of the cell, two at a time, until the number of carbon atoms is again greater than the initial number of carbon atoms. This entire process is repeated, cumulatively, for thousands of impacts per simulation, well beyond the required fluence for the cell to reach steady state. The total simulated fluence for each simulation is listed in table S1 of the supplementary information.

2.3. Simultaneous bombardment of Ar+ and neutral H

We also simulate simultaneous exposure to both Ar+ and H atoms. If the starting substrate is diamond, the cell is first bombarded with only ions to reduce the time to steady state. If the starting substrate is amorphous, then this initial step is skipped. Next, hydrogen neutrals are introduced to the top of the simulation cell at 2100 K, with velocity components drawn from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, to match the conditions

of the experiment done by Hopf et al [15]. The z component of the velocity is restricted to be negative so the inserted atom will move toward the surface. The simulation is then allowed to evolve for 0.1 ps before the addition of another neutral atom. Introduction of neutrals is paused every 36 neutrals to apply a stratified thermostat for 0.5 ps. The simulation continues until a monolayer of neutrals has been introduced (a monolayer (ML) is defined as 1.6 × 1015 atoms cm−2, or 72 atoms for a 6 × 6 simulation cell.) After this, an ion impact is simulated as described in the previous paragraph, another thermostat is applied, and the entire process is repeated until the desired fluence of ions is reached. The total simulated fluence for each simulation is listed in table S1 of the supplementary information.

2.4. Analysis

Confidence intervals were primarily calculated by bootstrapping on block averages of a single trajectory. In other words, a single cumulative simulation was run for each case (e.g. for each energy, potential, etc). Once the simulation reached steady state, relevant values (e.g. hydrogen uptake, number of amorphous carbon) were recorded after every ML of fluence. Values were averaged in blocks to create independent samples, and these samples were fed into a bootstrapping algorithm to determine the confidence intervals. Not all confidence intervals were determined in this manner, though. For simulations which use an amorphous substrate, the amount of time the simulation can remain at steady state without reaching the diamond subsurface is limited, so block averages from the steady-state periods of three separate simulations are combined for bootstrapping. The exact block widths and fluences considered are outlined in table S1 of the supplementary information. Finally, confidence intervals for etch product distributions shown in figure 10 are based on the binomial distribution and are calculated using the etch products observed during the entire steady-state period. More precise details about how these error bars are calculated can be found in the supplementary information or the published plotting code [16]. We use three different metrics to describe the amorphous layer formed in these simulations: number of amorphous carbon atoms (measured in ML), amorphous layer thickness (measured in Å) and amorphous layer range (also measured in Å). To identify which atoms are in the diamond cubic phase, and by extension which are amorphous carbon, common neighbor analysis is performed on the second neighbors of each atom [17]. Every carbon atom identified to be diamond cubic by this technique, as well as its first and second neighbors, are counted as diamond, and all others are considered amorphous. This analysis is implemented as a LAMMPS compute using code from OVITO [18]. To determine amorphous layer thickness, we define the amorphous layer as the region where carbon density, as determined by summing Gaussian kernels with σ = a/8 centered at each atomic position, is between 10% and 90% that of diamond. This metric was designed to provide a measure of the amorphous layer that ignored the fluctuating ‘stringy’ structures that form above the surface, and which could be compared to

## 3. Results and discussion

3.1. Comparison to Ar+ and Ar+/H beam experiments

For the first comparison between MD simulations and experiments, we use results of beam experiments from Hopf et al [15], Guzman de la Mata [19], Karahashi et al [20], and Cong et al [21]. In beam experiments, surfaces are exposed to known fluxes of species at controlled energies and the effects of these exposures are measured. Hopf et al used a ‘hard’ hydrocarbon film with a H/C ratio of 0.3, Karahashi et al used a carbon film containing essentially no hydrogen and a density of 1.85 g cm−3, Guzman de la Mata et al used a single crystal high pressure high temperature (HPHT) diamond substrate, and Cong et al used a polycrystalline diamond substrate grown in a PECVD reactor. For this set of comparisons we use the REBO2 C-H potentials in the MD simulations. Figure 1(a) plots predicted amorphous layer thickness for an initially crystalline diamond substrate as a function of Ar+ fluence for ion energies ranging from 50 eV to 200 eV. The amorphous layer thickness, as defined in the ‘Analysis’ section, is indicated by the dashed lines on the snapshot insets to figure 1(a). A steady state amorphous layer thickness is observed from the simulations after about 50 ML of Ar+ fluence for energies above about 100 eV. Figure 1(b) plots the approximate steady state amorphous layer thickness as a function of ion energy as well as the estimated thicknesses from the spectroscopic ellipsometry measurements of Cong et al [21]. The agreement between MD simulations and estimated measured thicknesses is good. We note that a similar Ar+

induced amorphization of initially crystalline Si was reported by Humbird et al [22], although the thickness of the amorphous diamond surfaces is smaller than that of Si for a given Ar+ energy. This is as expected since diamond is significantly harder than Si. A second important test of the MD simulations can be made by comparing steady state Ar+ sputtering yields and Ar+/H etch yields with experimental values. Figure 2 plots both of these quantities. The comparison between physical sputtering yields (average number of C atoms removed per incident Ar+) shows that the MD predictions are within the three sets of

experimental data from Hopf et al [15], Karahashi et al [20], and Guzman de la Mata et al [19]. It should be noted that the Hopf et al data were taken using a hydrogenated C film, the Karahashi et al data were taken using a nearly pure carbon film, and that both the MD simulations and the Guzman de la Mata et al data correspond to a diamond carbon substrate. But the Ar+ physical sputtering yields are similar for these materials under these conditions. The etch yield results from Hopf et al [15] from exposing the hydrogenated C substrate to a combined flux of Ar+ and H atoms, as expected, are about an order of magnitude higher than sputtering yield for Ar+ alone. Figure 2 shows two sets of etch yield results from MD simulations for this case. The squares correspond to predicted yield when the target is a preamorphized diamond substrate. This should correspond most closely to the experimental system in which a hydrogenated carbon film is the target. Calculated etch yields were scaled by 2.21 to adjust for differences in flux ratio between simulation and experiment (72 and 400, respectively) according to the flux ratio dependence reported by Hopf et al [15]. For comparison to subsequent calculations, shown below, involving H+-only impacts, figure 3 shows the layer side views after diamond is impacted with Ar+/H for energies ranging from 50 eV to 200 eV. In particular, the mixed near-surface regions with non-diamond carbon and H mixed together are relatively compact. Except for the point at 20 eV in figure 2, the agreement between the MD simulations using the pre-amorphized diamond target and the experiment is reasonably good. The relatively high measured yield value at 20 eV is difficult to explain and may require further investigation. In most ‘reactive ion etching’ observations for other materials (e.g. Si), we would expect 20 eV to be near or below the minimum ion energy threshold to induce etching (e.g. Vella et al [23]). It is possible that the relatively high apparent etch yield corresponding to 20 eV ions is due to a higher spontaneous etch yield for 0.2 eV H atoms than is accounted for in the simulations. But this interpretation would be inconsistent with the low etch yields associated with H+ ions at energies below about 5 eV as reported in the next section. The closed circles in figure 2 correspond to MD simulation results utilizing a diamond carbon substrate. At 100 eV and above, these results are nearly identical to the MD predictions using the pre-amorphized diamond layer (solid squares). It appears that the surface nanostructure affects etch yields significantly when ion energy approaches the threshold ion energy. We conclude from this section that the comparison between MD simulations using REBO2 potentials and experiment when surfaces are exposed to either Ar+ alone or to simultaneous fluxes of Ar+ and H atoms is generally good. The quality of the agreement is comparable to that observed in other systems (e.g. Si etching by Cl and Ar+ as reported by Vella et al [14, 23] and SiO2 etching [24]). As will be seen in the subsequent section, however, the agreement when energetic H+

is employed is less straightforward to interpret and appears to offer some unique challenges to the conventional use of MD simulations of plasma–surface interactions with REBO-style potentials.

3.2. Comparison of MD simulations to H+ beam experiments

To validate simulations where hydrogen is the sole energetic species etching or modifying the diamond surface, it would be ideal to compare simulations to experiments utilizing a well

characterized H+ ion beam system with a diamond substrate. Unfortunately, there appears to be few if any published experimental data for diamond substrate etch yields in the presence of characterized beams of H+ ions. There are, however, results for the effects of H+ ion beams on graphitic carbon surfaces, motivated primarily by interests in plasma-materials interactions in the plasma fusion community.

H+ ions with energies above a few eV will amorphize and hydrogenate the near-surface of the diamond substrate, suggesting that MD simulations of energetic H on diamond substrates will be similar to results for an amorphous target. But as we saw in the previous section, the identity of the underlying substrate can influence results when the energetic species impact at relatively low, near-threshold energies. Nevertheless, comparing MD results to these available experimental data was important in revealing some important apparent limitations to the use of REBO2 potentials for this application.

We have chosen to use the results of beam experiments from Mech et al [25] and Balden and Roth [26] to compare to MD simulations. Mech et al employed quadrupole mass spectrometer (QMS) estimates of etch products to obtain etch yields, and Balden and Roth employed direct substrate weight loss measurements. Both sets of investigators made similar, critical observations: (i) etch yield energy threshold for H+−C reactive ion etching is between 5–10 eV for normal incidence ions; and (ii) etch yield rises to a few percent and then remains approximately constant up to about 50 eV. This behavior of nearly constant yield with respect to impacting ion energy is qualitatively different from results observed in other systems in reactive ion etching or plasma etching. The etch yield vs. ion energy profiles illustrated in figure 2 are more typical. That is, above some threshold energy, yields rise approximately as the square root of ion energy.

The differences in the range of the amorphous layers and the corresponding differences in layer structure can be seen more clearly in the following two figures. Figure 8 plots the range of the amorphous layer vs ion fluence for 30 eV ions using both potentials. Circles indicate minimum and maximum ranges for both simulations. Side views of these cells at the highlighted minimum and maximum values of range are shown in figure 9. Horizontal lines on figure 9 show the positions of the lowest and highest amorphous carbon atoms. The left column in figure 9 shows results from a simulation performed with REBO2, and the right column shows from a simulation performed with REBO2-S. The REBO2 layers feature large, open, stringy structures above denser amorphous sub surfaces, while even the largest REBO2-S layer is still a coherent, interconnected bundle.

These large, stringy structures characteristic of layers using REBO2 mean more carbon is open and vulnerable to hydrogen impact. While the same surface area of carbon is subject to the initial hydrogen impact in both cases (since the hydrogen

enters normal to the amorphous surface), hydrogen’s small mass means relatively little energy is lost on its first collision, and deflected hydrogen remains significantly labile. In some cases, hydrogen can even become more reactive upon reflection. This is because more of its kinetic energy can be transferred, and thus far more chemistry can occur, in inelastic, bond-forming collisions, which only occur if the hydrogen ions are moving slowly enough to be captured by the dangling bond.

The stringy, open surfaces associated with REBO2 provide a larger surface area for these reflected hydrogen to attack. Stringiness will lead to strands or chunks of carbon that can be removed by breaking relatively few bonds. This will increase etch yields by removing more carbon per etching event. Figure 10 confirms that clusters larger than three carbon atoms contribute significantly to the observed yield from REBO2 simulations, while they are relatively unimportant in the REBO2-S simulations. The largest product seen in the 25 eV simulation performed with REBO2-S contained only 10 carbon atoms, while a simulation on the same cell size performed with REBO2 saw an etch product containing 91 carbon atoms. REBO2 etch yield distributions exhibit a long tail, showing how large etch products contribute significantly to the observed etch yields. By contrast, REBO2-S distributions show little to no contribution from products larger than 3 carbon atoms. Etch product distributions are discussed further in the supplementary information section.

The larger cutoff of REBO2-S implies that clusters must be farther from the nominal surface before being removed and counted as etch products in the simulation. It also means that simulations must increase the time per impact, since hydrogen must start farther from the surface. Both of these effects could create artifacts in the etching statistics. It has been verified that these changes do not in fact significantly affect the etch yield by repeating the 25 eV REBO2 simulation with the settings for the REBO2-S cluster cutoff and impact time. Etch yield was only slightly lower in this case, within statistical uncertainty.

## 4. Conclusions

Classical MD simulations were performed with the goal of deepening our understanding of plasma-assisted diamond etching. This is especially important when processing diamond for quantum sensing devices. This is because the performance of the device is extremely sensitive to atomic-scale defects in the near-surface region of the diamond. Therefore, in order to develop and improve plasmaassisted processing techniques of diamond, a fundamental understanding of the relevant plasma–surface interactions is needed.

Several interatomic force fields for diamond were examined in this work. Results are primarily reported for a secondgeneration REBO potential (referred to as REBO2) and a screened REBO potential (referred to as REBO2-S). Results for other potentials can be found in the supplementary information. The relative accuracy of REBO2 versus REBO2-S is assessed by comparing to literature data from beam experiments. REBO2 gives reasonable agreement with experiments for physical sputtering (etching only by Ar+ ions) and etching by hot (2100 K) H atoms and Ar+ ions. It is also demonstrated that amorphous C is more readily etched relative to diamond C.

A major qualitative difference in the behavior of the two potentials appears when considering etching by energetic H+

ions. While REBO2 and REBO2-S both give good agreement with experimental results at low ion energies (below and near threshold), REBO2 overestimates the etch yield at H+ ion energies above 10 eV. Furthermore, the REBO2 force field predicts that the etch yield will increase roughly linearly with the square root of the ion energy, while the experimental results shows completely different behavior. That is, the etch yield remains relatively constant even when the substrate is exposed to 30 eV H+ ion. It should be noted that this behavior

is atypical for an etch yield as a function of ion energy, and highlights some of the subtle complexities of diamond etch by H+ ions. On the other hand, simulations using REBO2- S show good agreement with the experimental etch yields. The difference in the performance of REBO2 and REBO2- S is attributed to the fact that REBO2-S better reproduces the near-surface amorphous layer created by H+ ion etch, keeping the layer more compact and interconnected relative to REBO2. This explanation is supported by careful analysis of the nearsurface region of the MD simulations.

A novel non-equilibrium plasma-driven processing technique is suggested by our simulation results for smoothing diamond surfaces. Given an initially rough diamond surface, exposure of the surface to Ar+ will amorphize and smooth the near-surface region. Next, the amorphous C can be removed via exposure to relatively low energy H+ ions. Given that it was shown that H more readily etches amorphous C as opposed to diamond C, we expect much of the amorphous layer to be etched away, thereby exposing the underlying diamond surface. However, simulations showed that there was still about 1 ML of amorphous hydrogenated carbon on the surface following the proposed method, possibly requiring an additional liquid etching step.

This study demonstrates the utility of using plasma to modify the near-surface region of diamond. Given the strict constraints on surface contamination and degree of atomicscale defects for quantum-grade diamond, plasma processing techniques show great promise in achieving the level of nearsurface quality needed and perhaps for speeding and/or simplifying processing. The qualitative difference in simulation predictions using REBO2 or REBO2-S highlights the difficultly of developing accurate, robust, and transferable interatomic force fields. The development and adoption of machinelearned interatomic potentials (such as DeepMD [52]) coupled with comparison to well-diagnosed beam experiments is

But in other contexts, such as higher temperatures or upon association with rigid surfaces, P. aeruginosa produces virulence factors that make it pathogenic towards C. elegans14–16. Many of P. aeruginosa’s effects on C. elegans are dynamic, as are C. elegans’ responses to P. aeruginosa. Naive C. elegans that have never previously encountered P. aeruginosa are attracted towards P. aeruginosa, and even prefer P. aeruginosa over other bacteria like Escherichia coli that are constitutively non-pathogenic towards C. elegans10,12,13. The speciﬁc molecule that mediates the attraction of C. elegans to P. aeruginosa was previously unknown. Here, we identify volatile ammonia, a byproduct of Pseudomonas aeruginosa nitrogen assimilation, as a key mediator of C. elegans attraction. Our studies highlight the importance of nitrogen metabolism in P. aeruginosa’s interactions with C. elegans. Nitrogen is essential for amino acid synthesis and also plays important roles in a variety of other processes17–19. Like all animals, C. elegans cannot directly utilize inorganic nitrogen sources like ammonium and must, therefore, obtain processed organic nitrogen from the proteins and amino acids in their bacterial food sources17,20. In contrast, bacteria like Pseudomonas species can process inorganic environmental ammonium into organic nitrogen21–24. Inorganic nitrogen is typically found in two forms: ammonium and nitrate. When ammonium is abundant, it is the preferred nitrogen source and is reduced into glutamine and glutamate, which subsequently function as intracellular organic nitrogen donors19. When ammonium availability is limited, most Pseudomonas species induce a process known as nitrogen assimilation, where they reduce environmental nitrate into ammonium, which can then be further reduced into glutamine and glutamate21–24. Although many studies have interrogated nitrogen assimilation pathways across diverse bacterial species, its importance in transkingdom communication and bacterial host interactions remains largely unknown. Here, we combine P. aeruginosa and C. elegans genetics to help bridge a gap in trans-kingdom signaling by linking animal chemosensation with bacterial metabolism and physiology. Our data show that volatile ammonia is produced by P. aeruginosa nitrogen assimilation, which is regulated by a small RNA (sRNA)-mediated transcriptional termination and anti-termination mechanism. Ammonia produced by P. aeruginosa is an attractant for C. elegans and causes them to speciﬁcally prefer P. aeruginosa over E. coli. Finally, we found that nitrogen assimilation affects the ability of P. aeruginosa to colonize C. elegans, which affects pathogenesis and demonstrates the importance of metabolism in trans-kingdom signaling and host-microbe interactions.

Results Disrupting the P11 sRNA perturbs the naive attraction of C. elegans to PA14 Within their natural habitat, C. elegans are surrounded by diverse bacterial species1–3. Previous studies have demonstrated that naive, untrained C. elegans are attracted to P. aeruginosa PA14 (PA14) and prefer it to E. coli OP50 (OP50)10,12,13. P11, also known as NalA in PA0124, is a sRNA previously shown to be necessary for a process in which trained C. elegans use transgenerational epigenetic inheritance to learn to avoid PA14 for four generations10,25. The role of P11 in the attraction of naive C. elegans to PA14 has not been previously examined. In the PA14 genome, P11 is found immediately upstream of an operon that mediates the ﬁrst step of nitrogen assimilation, including the two subunits of nitrite reductase (NirB and NirD), and nitrate reductase (NasC). Given that P11 is upstream of the nitrogen assimilation operon that produces ammonium and that ammonium-related compounds have been previously shown to affect worm chemotaxis7, we sought to interrogate P11 function in naive worm chemotaxis.

We examined the role of P11 in mediating the attraction of C. elegans to PA14 using an OP50 vs. PA14 bacterial choice assay (Fig. 1a, b). We ﬁrst conﬁrmed the previous ﬁnding that naive C. elegans prefer PA14 to OP50. We then performed choice assays between a PA14 strain with an ~150 base pair deletion surrounding P11 (ΔP11) and OP50. We found that ΔP11 eliminated the preference of PA14 over OP50 (Fig. 1b), suggesting that in the absence of P11, PA14 lacks the attractant that mediates preference over OP50.

Worms are attracted to the PA14 nitrogen assimilation metabolite, ammonia To gain insight into the nature of the P11-dependent signal produced by PA14, we ﬁrst interrogated the mechanism by which C. elegans responds to this signal. Both the AWA and AWC neurons facilitate worm chemotaxis to volatile compounds, whereas the ASE neuron is involved in taste sensation4,26. To determine which neuron mediates attraction to PA14, we subjected worms with individual mutants that affect these neurons to choice assays between wild-type PA14 (WT) and ΔP11. Like wild-type C. elegans, worms defective in the function of ASE (che-1(p672))27 or AWA (odr-7(ky4))28 preferred WT PA14 to PA14 ΔP11. However, che-2(e1033) mutants, which are defective in the function of ciliated neurons including AWA, AWB, AWC, and others29, no longer exhibited a preference (Fig. 1c, left). Because che-2(e1033) disrupts the function of all ciliated neurons29, we examined additional mutants defective in the functions of speciﬁc subsets of these neurons. Worm mutants defective in AWB (ceh-37(ok642))30,31 or AWC and ASE (ceh- 36(ky646))30 still preferred WT PA14 over PA14 ΔP11. However, a worm mutant defective in the functions of AWB and AWC (odr-1(n1936))31 did not demonstrate a preference (Fig. 1c, right).These results suggest that P11-dependent attraction to PA14 is mediated by a volatile odorant and are consistent with a previous study that did not identify the speciﬁc attractant C. elegans use for naive chemotaxis to P. aeruginosa but did show that this preference is mediated by the AWB-AWC circuit13. Nitrogen assimilation produces ammonium, which can spontaneously convert to a volatile form, ammonia32. Thus, if the deletion surrounding P11 disrupts nitrogen assimilation, it might reduce ammonia production. To determine if the P11 deletion disrupted nitrogen assimilation, we assayed the ability of ΔP11 to grow in nitrogen-free media supplemented with inorganic nitrates. WT PA14 grew robustly in these conditions, but ΔP11 mutants did not (Supplementary Fig. 1a). We conﬁrmed that this growth defect was due to an inability to reduce nitrate by demonstrating that adding the products of the nitrogen assimilation reactions (ammonium, Glu, or Gln) rescued PA14 ΔP11 growth (Supplementary Fig. 1b–e). We also conﬁrmed that the ΔP11 mutant lacked expression of the downstream nitrogen assimilation genes, providing a molecular explanation for its nitrogen assimilation defect (Supplementary Fig. 1f). Given that the P11 deletion disrupts nitrogen assimilation, we next sought to directly determine the effect of this mutant on ammonia production. For this purpose, we adapted a colorimetric ammonia assay so that it could be used in the surface-associated conditions employed for C. elegans choice assays. We found that ΔP11 produced statistically signiﬁcantly less ammonia than WT PA14 in the conditions in which we assayed bacterial choice preference (Fig. 1d). We also demonstrated that ammonia is sufﬁcient to promote C. elegans attraction by conﬁrming previous ﬁndings that C. elegans is attracted to ammonia and that this attraction requires the function of the ciliated sensory neurons that detect volatile odorants7 (Fig. 1e, f). To determine if ammonia sensing is necessary for C. elegans’ PA14 preference, we exposed C. elegans to saturating levels of exogenous ammonia, which should eliminate any ammonia gradients produced by bacteria in this environment. In the presence of saturating concentrations of ammonia, we found that C. elegans no longer preferred WT PA14 to OP50 or ΔP11 (Fig. 1g–i). Therefore, our data suggest that P11-dependent ammonia production is necessary and sufﬁcient to explain naive C. elegans’ attraction to PA14.

A complex regulatory mechanism controls PA14 nitrogen assimilation The mutant referred to as “ΔP11” both above and in prior studies10

deletes >150 bp of the genomic region that resides between two operons implicated in nitrogen assimilation (Fig. 2a). We thus examined mutants in these operons to dissect their functions in nitrogen assimilation. As expected, transposon insertions in either nitrite reductase, nirB, or nitrate reductase, nasC, rendered PA14 unable to grow in conditions in which nitrates are the sole nitrogen source (Supplementary Fig. 2a). These mutants also affected C. elegans attraction: C. elegans preferred WT PA14 to nirBTn or nasCTn. Loss of nirB or nasC was also sufﬁcient to completely explain the ΔP11 C. elegans attraction defect, as C. elegans showed no preference between ΔP11 and nirBTn or nasCTn (Fig. 2b). Upstream of P11 is another operon containing two regulatory genes, nasS and nasT. In a closely related Pseudomonas strain, PA01, it has been shown that NasT can bind to either the P11-containing 5’ leader region of the nirB gene (P11) or to NasS in a mutually exclusive manner24. P11 contains a predicted hairpin that terminates transcription when unbound, and NasT binding to the leader is required for downstream transcription of nirB, nirD, and nasC. Meanwhile, NasS

mutually exclusively binds to either NasT or to nitrate. Thus, in the absence of nitrates, NasS binds to NasT, which leaves P11 unbound and results in termination that prevents nirBD nasC expression. When nitrates are present, nitrates bind to NasS, freeing NasT to bind to P11 and promote nirBD nasC expression24 (Fig. 2a). To determine if PA14 nitrogen assimilation is also regulated by this partner-switching regulatory mechanism24, we assayed PA14 nasS and nasT mutants for their ability to grow in nitrogen-free media supplemented with nitrates. Whereas nasSTn grew as well as WT PA14, nasTTn was unable to grow (Supplementary Fig. 2a). We also analyzed the expression of both the P11 and nirB RNA’s by qRT-PCR in surface-attached conditions mimicking those used during C. elegans choice assays. We found that nasTTn dramatically reduced the downstream nirB gene to undetectable levels but retained relatively high P11 levels. While nasSTn exhibited similar P11 levels to those seen in nasTTn, the levels of nirB were signiﬁcantly higher in nasSTn than in nasTTn (Fig. 2c). These results suggest that the NasT-NasS partner-switching mechanism regulates nitrate/nitrite reductase expression in PA14, providing a molecular explanation for their effects on nitrogen assimilation. The speciﬁcity and relevance of worm attraction to Pseudomonas-produced ammonia While our results thus far are consistent with bacterially produced ammonia representing the attractant that drives worm chemoattraction to P. aeruginosa, the speciﬁcity and relevance of this behavior remained unclear. For example, saturating ammonia disrupted the preference for P. aeruginosa, but it is formally possible that saturating ammonia nonspeciﬁcally disrupts all C. elegans chemoattraction. To address this possibility, we assessed the effect of saturating ammonia on worm attraction towards benzaldehyde, another known worm attractant31. Regardless of the presence of saturating ammonia, worms were still able to sense and locomote toward benzaldehyde, suggesting that sensing and chemotaxis towards other attractants is not disrupted by saturating levels of ammonia (Fig. 3a). As another test of odorant speciﬁcity, we challenged worms to a bacterial choice assay between WT PA14 and ΔP11 or nirBTn in the presence of saturating concentrations of benzaldehyde. Worms still preferred WT PA14 over PA14 mutants defective in nitrogen assimilation expression (Fig. 3b), demonstrating that worms can speciﬁcally identify differential levels of ammonia produced by PA14 in the presence of saturating levels of another attractant. It was previously shown that PA14 can produce cues such as 1-undecene and blue light (pyocyanin) that are avoided by naive worms8,33. Although our data suggest that PA14 nitrogen assimilation is involved in naive worm attraction to PA14, it is plausible that nitrogen assimilation can also affect avoidance behaviors in naive worms. To assess the speciﬁcity of ammonia for worm attraction, we employed worm avoidance assays to WT PA14 and PA14 strains defective in nitrogen assimilation (PA14 ΔP11 and nirBTn). Our data show that worms avoid PA14 lawns at the same rate regardless of a functional

PA14 nitrogen assimilation pathway (Fig. 3c). Thus, nitrogen assimilation appears to affect C. elegans attraction to P. aeruginosa, but does not affect repulsion from other previously described cues. PA14 is a human clinical isolate that is not an abundant Pseudomonas species in the natural soil environments typically encountered by C. elegans. Therefore, we sought to determine if ammonia’s role as a chemoattractant is speciﬁc to PA14 or if ammonia might also play a role in worm attraction to soil-resident Pseudomonas species that might be more physiologically relevant for C. elegans’ natural environment. We performed choice assays between OP50 and Pseudomonas vranovensis or Pseudomonas mendocina, both of which are soilresident Pseudomonas species and are preferred by naive worms over OP503,34,35 (Fig. 3d). Similar to the behavior we observed for PA14, worm preference towards each of these Pseudomonas species was abolished by the presence of saturating ammonia, suggesting that worms also use ammonia sensing to chemotax to natural isolates of Pseudomonas (Fig. 3d).

Two P11 stem-loops inversely regulate nitrogen assimilation expression RNA secondary structure formation is important for numerous RNA functions. The predicted secondary structure of P11 contains stem loops (Fig. 4a), which often facilitate protein-RNA interactions or function as transcriptional terminators36–38. To determine the functions of the P11 stem-loops and to better understand the mechanism by which P11 regulates the nitrogen assimilation operon, we made two mutants that each speciﬁcally deleted one of the stem-loops (P11mut1 and P11mut2) (Fig. 4a, b). Unlike the large ΔP11 deletion described above, these small mutations do not extend upstream into the operon promoter. PA14 P11mut1 failed to grow in nitrogen-free media supplemented with nitrate (Supplementary Fig. 2f), suggesting that deletion of the ﬁrst stem-loop leads to a loss of expression of the nitrogen assimilation enzymes. To understand the cause of this nitrogen assimilation phenotypic defect, we examined the expression of both the P11 leader region and the downstream nirB gene. P11mut1 retained robust P11 expression, indicating that the operon promoter remained intact. However, nirB mRNA expression was so low as to remain undetectable in P11mut1 (Fig. 4c). These results suggest that P11mut1 results in transcriptional termination between P11 and nirB, which could be explained by loss of NasT binding, resulting in a loss of antitermination activity. Conversely, P11mut2 grew robustly in nitrogenfree media supplemented with nitrate (Supplementary Fig. 2f) and retained relatively high levels of both P11 and nirB expression (Fig. 4c). These data suggest that disrupting the second stem-loop leads to constitutive expression of nirB. The second P11 stem-loop is followed by a poly-T sequence, a hallmark indicator of a rho-independent terminator38. Thus, our results support the hypothesis that within P11, the ﬁrst stem-loop is the site of anti-termination by NasT, and the second stem-loop functions as a rho-independent terminator that leads to transcriptional termination when NasT is not bound. To examine the phenotypic consequences of stem-loop mutations, we subjected C. elegans to choice assays between WT PA14 and the two P11 stem-loop mutants. WT PA14 was preferred over P11mut1, whereas no preference was exhibited between WT PA14 and P11mut2 (Fig. 4d). When given the choice between P11mut1 and P11mut2, P11mut2 was preferred (Fig. 4d). We also tested worm preference between the P11 mutants and nirBTn, nasCTn, nasSTn, and nasTTn. Worms did not prefer P11mut1 over nirBTn, nasCTn, or nasTTn (Fig. 4e). However, nasSTn was more attractive than P11mut1 (Fig. 4e). The opposite effect was observed when comparing mutants in all these genes to P11mut2, i.e., worms preferred P11mut2 over nirBTn, nasCTn, and nasTTn, but did not prefer P11mut2 to nasSTn (Fig. 4f). Finally, we tested ammonia production in the P11 mutants and found that ammonia levels were reduced in P11mut1 but were normal in P11mut2 (Fig. 4g). Nitrogen assimilation is important for PA14 ﬁtness during worm infections Our ﬁndings demonstrate that the nitrogen assimilation pathway affects the attraction of C. elegans towards PA14, but a previous study also demonstrated that the large ΔP11 deletion affects the pathogenesis of PA14 towards C. elegans10. To determine if the pathogenesis defect of ΔP11 is due to this mutant’s defect in nitrogen assimilation, we assayed C. elegans survival in the presence of a speciﬁc mutant in nitrite reductase, nirBTn, as well as in a P11 mutant that does not disrupt the nitrogen assimilation operon promoter, P11mut1. C. elegans infected by nirBTn and P11mut1 survived signiﬁcantly longer than worms infected by WT PA14 (Fig. 5a). To assess whether the pathogenesis defect is speciﬁcally due to nitrogen assimilation, we supplemented infected worms with glutamine, a preferred nitrogen source that

Nitrogen assimilation is an energetically expensive pathway19, which may explain why P. aeruginosa PA14 has evolved multiple regulatory components to tightly control its expression. NasS and NasT function in a partner-switching mechanism in response to intracellular inorganic nitrates. By binding to P11, NasT facilitates transcriptional anti-termination of the nitrogen assimilation operon, allowing PA14 to reduce inorganic nitrates into ammonium and, subsequently, glutamine and glutamate. This multifaceted approach to regulating nitrogen assimilation ensures a proper balance between energy conservation and growth in a speciﬁc environment. Interestingly, our results demonstrate that one such environment where

nitrogen assimilation is important for bacterial growth is within the C. elegans body at later stages of infection. While it is impossible to rule out all secondary functions, our data suggest that P11’s roles in regulating nitrogen assimilation and bacterial growth are sufﬁcient to explain the pathogenesis defect associated with the loss of P11. These data highlight the importance of considering environmental regulation and metabolism in the context of understanding bacterial ﬁtness and pathogenesis during infections. In the future, assaying bacterial load and metabolism within animals may help to untangle the roles of other factors in contributing to either bacterial growth in that environment or speciﬁc virulence pathways.

In addition to shedding light on the role of P11 in bacteria, our ﬁndings provide insights into how C. elegans interact with bacteria in their environment. Previous studies examining molecules produced by P. aeruginosa and sensed by C. elegans identiﬁed several compounds that are repulsive to C. elegans and one molecule that is attractive, but without being able to eliminate production of these molecules from the bacteria the actual activity of these molecules remained unclear8,9,11,39. Excitingly, we identiﬁed the nitrogen assimilation product, ammonia, as the major attractant that causes C. elegans to prefer P. aeruginosa over E. coli. In addition to conﬁrming that ammonia is produced when P. aeruginosa attracts C. elegans, we demonstrate that ammonia sensing is necessary for C. elegans’ preference for P. aeruginosa, as well as other Pseudomonas species that are naturally encountered by C. elegans, over E. coli. Speciﬁcally, disrupting ammonia gradients by either saturating the environment with excess ammonia or using P. aeruginosa mutants defective in ammonia production, inhibits C. elegans attraction. A recent study identiﬁed a second nitrite reductase gene, nirA, in P. aeruginosa PA0140. It is possible that the residual ammonia we observed to be produced by nirB mutants could be due to the activity of nirA24,39. Future work to untangle the conditions in which nirA expression occurs and its impact on P. aeruginosa ammonia production andC. elegans interactions could further illuminate the complex mechanisms by which P. aeruginosa and C. elegans interact. Worms rely on sensory information to ﬁnd vital resources like nitrogen-based compounds, and bacteria provide rich nutrient sources20,31. Pseudomonads comprise the largest subgroup of the bacterial genre within the C. elegans natural microbiome1–3. Many Pseudomonads produce ammonia but are not harmful to C. elegans, and many other non-pathogenic soil-based bacteria also possess nitrogen assimilation machinery3,21–23,41–44. Therefore, we hypothesize that the beneﬁts of being attracted to nutrient sources signaled by ammonia production may generally outweigh the risk to C. elegans of becoming infected by a pathogen. If C. elegans does encounter a pathogen like P. aeruginosa, pathogenesis is regulated in a complex manner such that the bacteria could be present in a non-pathogenic state14–16. And even when P. aeruginosa is pathogenic, it often takes several days to kill C. elegans, during which time C. elegans can continue to produce offspring. Those offspring will have been taught to move away from P. aeruginosa due to the P11-mediated and other learned avoidance mechanisms10,12,45, giving them a chance to survive and ﬁnd alternative food sources in the next generation. Future studies interrogating nitrogen assimilation and ammonia production in different bacteria and how they inﬂuence C. elegans chemotaxis will shed further light on the generality of these processes. For example, while our studies suggest that the pathogenesis defect associated with nitrogen assimilation mutants is due to the impact of these processes on bacterial growth, it remains possible that they also inﬂuence virulence pathways more directly. Our work highlights the complexity of trans-kingdom signaling: the same bacterial pathways that are important for C. elegans to acquire essential nutrients appear to also be important for the growth of harmful bacteria within C. elegans. The fact that untrained C. elegans prefer PA14 suggests that in the short term, the need to ﬁnd nutrients is prioritized over the risk of encountering a pathogen. However, C. elegans have also evolved mechanisms to avoid harmful bacteria in future generations after ingesting them10,12,25,35. Interestingly, in PA14 these behaviors are coupled in that the same sRNA that mediates transgenerationally inherited-learned avoidance of PA14 is also required for naive C. elegans attraction to PA14 by regulating ammonia production. In this manner, C. elegans may use chemotaxis as a simple form of an adaptive immune system that speciﬁcally learns to avoid harmful pathogens only once they are encountered. This system of combining ammonia sensing and sRNA-mediated adaptive avoidance enables C. elegans to identify food reservoirs and then avoid pathogens with speciﬁcity.

# Benford’s Law: applications to chondrules and refractory inclusions

Jake Grodner1 · Alan E. Rubin2,3

Received: 15 July 2024 / Accepted: 3 January 2025

© The Author(s) 2025 OPEN

Abstract Benford’s Law is a scale- and base-invariant probability distribution wherein smaller numerals occur more often than higher numerals as the first digits in many large, naturally occurring datasets. In the present study, the areas of individual meteoritic chondrules and refractory inclusions were tested for conformity to Benford’s Law. Datasets of chondrule, CAI, and AOA sizes from CO and CV carbonaceous chondrites from the literature were analyzed. In each dataset, the set of areas of all inclusions (chondrules and refractory inclusions combined) was found to conform most closely to Benford’s Law. The area distributions are approximately log normal; they are positively skewed with decreasing numerical values from mean to median to mode. The conformity of the set of all chondrules and refractory inclusions to Benford’s Law suggests that Benford’s Law may apply to the process of aerodynamic sorting in the protoplanetary disk prior to the agglomeration of chondritic planetesimals.

Keywords  Meteorites · Benford’s Law · Chondrules · Refractory inclusions · Nebular sorting

While there is currently no comprehensive theory that explains the ubiquity of Benford’s Law [13], there have been many attempts to describe its common occurrence. The Law was first noticed by astronomer Simon Newcomb [14], who found that in books of logarithmic tables, pages with first digit 1 were the most worn, and that the wear of pages decreased with increasing size of the first digit. Frank Benford, a physicist at the General Electric Company, rediscovered the probability distribution (which is now named after him), and found it applied to a wide range of datasets, including those consisting of atomic weights, street addresses, and river surface areas [2]. Later, Hill [1] provided a new statistical derivation, similar to the Central Limit Theorem, essentially stating that if random samples are taken from random probability distributions in a scale-invariant way, the first digit frequencies of the sample will tend towards a Benford’s Law-like distribution. Deviation from Benford’s Law in datasets expected to exhibit conformity can lead to insights about the data. It may indicate that the dataset is not representative of a complete population that might otherwise conform to Benford’s Law; alternatively, deviations may indicate alteration of the original sample distribution (e.g., [15]). Furthermore, just as Benford’s Law has been used to detect tampering in tax returns [3], Benford’s Law analysis of datasets describing natural phenomena can also help detect “tampering” by physical processes. For instance, Rubin [15] analyzed a database of the masses of ordinary-chondrite meteorites and found that deviation from Benford’s Law was caused in part by the effects of terrestrial weathering, which modified the original mass distribution after atmospheric fragmentation of the meteoroid progenitors. We investigated whether Benford’s Law applies to the principal mafic and refractory components of carbonaceous chondrites—chondrules, calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (CAIs, a.k.a. refractory inclusions), and ameboid olivine aggregates (AOAs) [16]. Chondrules are spheroidal objects mainly composed of olivine and pyroxene crystals embedded in silico-feldspathic material (e.g., [16]). They constitute between 20 vol.% and 80 vol.% of chondrites, except for CI chondrites (which are chondrule-free) [17]. Chondrules range in size over four orders of magnitude, from less than 1 µm to greater than 1 cm; they are typically a few hundred micrometers in diameter [18]. While the origin of chondrules remains an area of ongoing research, one popular model of chondrule formation involves flash melting of dust aggregates in the solar nebula [16]. Refractory inclusions range in size from less than a millimeter to more than a centimeter; they are composed mainly of spinel, melilite, perovskite, hibonite, pyroxene, metallic Fe–Ni, anorthite, and olivine [19]. These are the oldest chondritic components that formed in the Solar System; they have absolute 207Pb-206Pb ages of 4.567—4.568 Ga [20, 21]. The similarly sized AOAs are irregularly shaped inclusions that contain major olivine, major-to-minor calcium pyroxene and minor anorthite (e.g., [22]). In addition to chondrules, CAIs, and AOAs, chondrites contain fine-grained silicate matrix material and coarse isolated grains of olivine and pyroxene (probably derived from fragmented chondrules). Also present in most chondrite groups are varying proportions of metallic Fe–Ni, sulfide, oxide, and phosphate (e.g., [16]). In this study, we explore whether the sizes of chondrules and refractory inclusions in CO and CV carbonaceous chondrites conform to Benford’s Law. If the inclusion sizes follow this distribution, any deviations among different datasets may provide insights into the formation or post-formation histories of these objects.

## 2  Analytical procedures

Numerical data were taken from Ebel et al. (2016) and Simon et al. [23]. The Ebel et al. dataset contains the areas (in square micrometers) of chondrules and other inclusions in CO, CV, and ungrouped carbonaceous chondrites. The CV chondrites include Allende, Tibooburra, Nova 002, Bali, Mokoia, Vigarano, and Leoville; the CO chondrites include Colony, Kainsaz, Ornans, Lancé, and Warrenton. We exclude Acfer 094 from Ebel et al. [24] because the meteorite is an ungrouped carbonaceous chondrite. The Ebel et al. study utilized an electron probe microanalyzer to create maps of slabs and polished sections, which were then imported into a drawing software program to determine sizes of inclusions and other properties. The Simon et al. dataset contains the diameters (in micrometers) of chondrules, CAIs, and AOAs in slabs of Allende, as well as the diameters of inclusions in the unique ungrouped chondrite, NWA 5717. In the Simon et al. study, images of the slabs were produced from SEM mapping and analyzed to determine the areas of individual inclusions. Circular diameters were calculated from these areas. Both datasets include the sizes of chondrules, CAIs, and AOAs; the Ebel et al. dataset also contains sizes of isolated olivine grains, metal grains, and metal-sulfide assemblages. Although Ebel et al. [24] did not characterize Al-rich chondrules as chondrules, we have included them with the other chondrules. Assuming the inclusions in the Simon et al. data set to be spherical, we calculated the areas of these inclusions from the given diameters (this should not introduce error, as the diameters were back-calculated from the 2D areas of the inclusions in the Simon et al. study [23]). The first digits of the inclusion areas in both the Ebel et al. and Simon et al. datasets (in square micrometers) were determined and counted. These counts of the frequency of leading digits 1 through 9 can be compared to Benford’s Law. All statistical properties in this study were calculated using the standard formulae in Microsoft Excel. The datasets used in this study rely on two-dimensional sectioning to measure inclusion sizes. Eisenhour [25] and Metzler [26] showed that 2D-sectioning leads to chondrule size-frequency distributions that underestimate chondrule diameters, primarily due to non-equatorial sectioning. Other studies discuss such 2D-sectioning effects more generically for particle sizes (e.g. [27]). Thus, the size distributions studied in this paper are likely shifted towards smaller sizes, which may limit the robustness of conclusions drawn from these distributions. The creation of algorithms to correct size distributions deduced from 2D-sectioning is an active field of research. While various methods have been proposed since the work of Dodd [28], Metzler [26] showed that many widely-used corrections to 2D size distributions overestimate chondrule sizes.

## 4  Discussion

Given the close conformity of chondrule sizes and CAI sizes to Benford’s Law, we first consider the origin of their respective size distributions to find processes potentially described by Benford’s Law. Jacquet [32] proposed that chondrule size distributions are shaped primarily by bouncing-limited sticking growth of preexisting aggregates. Numerical simulations by Arakawa et al. [33] showed that bouncing-limited growth of dust aggregates was widespread in the protoplanetary disk, and it seems possible that size distributions of various chondrite components, including chondrules and CAIs, may be derived from this process. If these results are accurate, bouncing-limited sticking growth could produce a Benford’s Law size distribution. Numerical simulations by Charnoz et al. [34] showed that collisional growth of CAIs through surface sticking creates a power law size distribution. These simulations, however, produce a power law size distribution with an exponent around -2.4 [34]. Pietronero et al. [35] showed that power law distributions with exponents less than -1 produce higher frequencies of leading digit 1s than to be expected from Benford’s Law. The size distributions from the Charnoz et al. simulations, then, likely deviates significantly from Benford’s Law. One may then consider the relatively close conformity of the Ebel et al. CAI sizes to Benford’s Law as a suggestion that collisional growth does not directly produce their observed size distribution. It should nevertheless be noted that the observed size distributions recorded by Charnoz et al. were estimated to follow a power law with a -2.99 to -2.7 exponent (after a correction for non-equatorial sectioning). Rubin [36, 37] noted that chondrite groups with large chondrules tend to have large CAIs and large AOAs. He suggested that aerodynamic size sorting in the nebula was at least partially responsible for the size distributions of these components. The datasets used in this analysis do not, however, represent the true size distribution of chondrules or refractory inclusions immediately after these particles formed in the solar nebula; instead, they represent the size distributions of chondrules and refractory inclusions found in chondrites. Chondrule formation produces a broader size distribution than found in meteorites, which is significantly modified by aerodynamic sorting [38]. Thus, the data studied here are insufficient evidence from which to draw conclusions concerning the processes of chondrule or refractory inclusion formation. After all, these objects formed in different regions of the nebula (chondrules locally throughout the nebula, CAIs near the Sun) [39] under different conditions of turbulence, dust/gas ratio, and (possibly) melting mechanism. It cannot be expected that similar size distributions would have been produced during chondrule and CAI formation. One cannot necessarily conclude that Benford’s Law applies to the set of chondrule sizes immediately after their formation. It is possible, however, that Benford’s Law may describe a different process; namely, aerodynamic sorting in the solar nebula. While the size distributions of chondrules and refractory inclusions may be limited by formation processes, the aerodynamic size sorting in the nebula may determine their distribution in chondrites [40]. Although the simulations by Jacquet [32] seem to contradict the deterministic role of aerodynamic processes in the origin of these size distributions, many workers have concluded that chondrule size distributions were mainly determined by nebular sorting (e.g., [41]). Within each of the main datasets studied, the areas of all inclusions conform more closely to Benford’s Law than the sets of areas of each particular inclusion type (chondrules, AOAs, and CAIs). At first glance, the close conformity of the set of all inclusion sizes may be expected from the mathematical foundation of Benford’s Law; after all, one way to consider Benford’s Law distributions is that they are the result of compiling random samples from various random distributions [1]. One may consider the distribution of all inclusions as a sampling of the size distributions of each inclusion type. One may notice, however, that due to the effects of aerodynamic sorting, these distributions are not sampled randomly. There may therefore be a different interpretation of Benford’s Law’s application to the set of all inclusion areas. The fact that the set

That is, Benford’s Law may describe the size distribution produced by nebular sorting, in which different chondrite components are sorted together in the protoplanetary disk [42]. Although CAIs formed earlier than chondrules in a region much closer to the Sun, they were transported to greater heliocentric distances where they could have been sorted along with chondrules prior to the agglomeration of chondritic planetesimals (e.g., [39]). AOAs were similarly aerodynamically sorted [43]. Various aerodynamic properties of particles in the solar nebula, particularly radial velocity, are strongly dependent on particle size (e.g., [44]). These aerodynamic properties dictate the process of accumulation of larger bodies within the nebula [44], specifically, the collisional growth of smaller particles [45]. Since these processes related to aerodynamic sorting are size-dependent, and the size distribution produced by sorting is Benford-like, Benford’s Law may be a useful tool to describe the agglomeration of planetesimals. Because larger datasets are more likely to adhere to Benford’s Law [46], the significant deviation from Benford’s Law in the sets of AOA and CAI areas may be explained in part by the markedly lower sample sizes. This is supported by the fact that the CAI data set with the highest SSD value (Simon et al. CV data) represents a significantly smaller sample size than the other three datasets. The AOA area datasets, none of which display close conformity to Benford’s Law as per SSD, are notably smaller than any CAI or chondrule dataset in this study. These inferences about sample size mean that larger datasets of AOA areas may or may not yield closer conformity to Benford’s Law. There may be other sources of deviation from Benford’s Law than sample size. Simon et al. [23] noted that previous studies, including the Ebel et al. [24] study, may have suffered from sampling bias. However, by and large, the dataset that deviates the most from Benford’s Law is the CV data from Simon et al. [23]. Once again, though, the sample sizes are much smaller for this dataset. These datasets have other limitations. The data analyzed in this study represents only CO and CV meteorites; the results found herein may not apply to all chondrite groups. Although two-dimensional representations of three-dimensional objects could represent an additional source of error, the statistical adjustment to 3D should not affect the adherence of the datasets to Benford’s Law.

## 5  Conclusions

The set of chondrule areas and the set of the areas of all mafic and refractory inclusions in CO and CV meteorites display close conformity to Benford’s Law. Three of the four CO and CV sets of CAI areas also conform to Benford’s Law. The set of all inclusion areas conforms more closely to Benford’s Law than the set of areas of any particular type of inclusion. The close conformity of the areas of all inclusion types to Benford’s Law suggests that size sorting in the nebula of these components produces a Benford’s Law distribution.
